A pittance is a very small amount of money — so small that it feels unfair, insulting, or laughably inadequate compared to what was expected, deserved, or needed.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is that it doesn't just mean small. It means disappointingly and unacceptably small. There is always a sense of injustice or inadequacy baked into it.

For example, if you work 60 hours a week at a grueling job and get paid $2 an hour, you are being paid a pittance. The word captures not just the smallness of the amount, but the wrongness of it — the mismatch between what you put in and what you got back.

Pittance is not a neutral word. It carries a tone of dissatisfaction, frustration, or even outrage. When someone uses this word, they are not simply describing a small amount — they are making a judgment that the amount is beneath what is acceptable.

This is what separates pittance from simply saying "a little" or "a small amount." Compare these two sentences:

  • "She earned a small amount for her work."
  • "She earned a pittance for her work."

The first sentence is plain and factual. The second sentence tells you the same fact, but it also tells you that the amount was shockingly low — that she deserved far more, and that anyone hearing this should feel some sense of injustice on her behalf.
What It's Most Commonly Used With

Pittance is used most often with money — particularly wages, salaries, payments, allowances, and tips. The word fits naturally into situations where someone is being compensated for their time, effort, talent, or sacrifice, and the compensation falls drastically short.

Common situations where you'd hear it:

Workers who are underpaid. Artists or creators who are not fairly compensated for their work. Elderly people living on a tiny pension. Volunteers or interns receiving a token payment. Employees receiving a raise so small it's almost meaningless.

You will almost always see pittance used in a handful of predictable ways. The most common is "paid a pittance" or "earn a pittance." You'll also frequently see "a mere pittance" — where the word mere adds extra emphasis to just how small the amount is.

Here are natural examples:

  • "The factory workers were paid a pittance despite working 12-hour shifts."
  • "She sold her grandfather's rare coin collection for a pittance — she had no idea what it was worth."
  • "After years of loyal service, his retirement bonus was a mere pittance."
  • "The company made millions in profit but offered employees a pittance in raises."
  • "He worked as a freelance writer for years, earning a pittance."

Notice in all of these, there is always an implied contrast — between the effort, worth, or sacrifice on one side, and the inadequate payment on the other.

While money is by far its most common context, pittance can occasionally be used to describe a very small amount of anything — food, time, attention, credit, etc. — when the speaker wants to convey that the amount is insultingly small relative to what was needed or deserved.

  • "After the earthquake, the survivors were given a pittance of food and water."
  • "He gave a pittance of his time to his family despite promising to be more present."

This usage is less common, but completely correct and understood.
Whose Perspective Does It Come From?

Pittance is almost always used from the perspective of the person receiving (or the one sympathizing with the receiver). It is a word that sides with the underdog — the worker, the artist, the struggling person. You would rarely hear someone who is giving money describe their own payment as a pittance, because that would be an admission that they are being unfair.
How It Differs From Similar Words

A little / a small amount — purely descriptive, no emotion or judgment attached.

Trifle — also means something small and unimportant, but it's more about insignificance than injustice. A trifle is trivial. A pittance is unfair.

Peanuts (informal) — very similar in meaning and feel to pittance, but much more informal and casual. You'd use peanuts in casual speech; you'd use pittance in both casual and more formal or written contexts.

Next to nothing — a phrase meaning nearly zero; similar in meaning but lacks the specific emotional charge of injustice that pittance carries.

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: a pittance is an amount of money (or sometimes anything else) that is so small it feels unfair or insulting — far less than what was deserved or expected.
